understanding.intro: In the thirty years since, a series of breakthroughs led to the thinking machines we use every day.

nodes.name: Word embeddings
nodes.gist: Words became numbers a machine could compare, so similar meanings landed close together.

source.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space

nodes.name: The Transformer
nodes.gist: A model built on attention alone could weigh every word against every other, and train in parallel on far more text.

source.title: Attention Is All You Need

nodes.name: Few-shot prompting
nodes.gist: A large model could take on a new task from a few examples written as text, with no retraining.

source.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners

nodes.name: Instruction tuning
nodes.gist: Models trained on human feedback learned to do what people actually asked, so anyone could simply ask.

source.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback

finding.intro: Finding is still hard. The shortcuts are now learned from data, not written by hand.

nodes.name: PageRank
nodes.gist: Search results began to be ranked by who linked to whom, so the web’s own links decided which pages mattered.

source.title: The Anatomy of a Large-Scale Hypertextual Web Search Engine

nodes.name: Attention
nodes.gist: A model could learn which parts of its input matter for each step, instead of being told.

source.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate

nodes.name: Dense retrieval
nodes.gist: Questions and passages became points in one space, so the closest passages could be found by meaning.

source.title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering

nodes.name: Retrieval-augmented generation
nodes.gist: A model could look up relevant passages itself, then answer using what it found.

source.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

backtracking.intro: Backtracking is still how hard problems get solved. Now the machine learns when to do it.

nodes.name: Monte Carlo tree search
nodes.gist: A program could try many random lines of play and spend its effort on the branches that kept working.

source.title: Bandit based Monte-Carlo Planning

nodes.name: AlphaGo
nodes.gist: Networks trained on past games learned which branches were worth trying, so the shortcuts were no longer written by hand.

source.title: Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree search

nodes.name: Chain-of-thought prompting
nodes.gist: Language models reasoned far better when they wrote out their steps, so the search could happen in words.

source.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

nodes.name: Reasoning models
nodes.gist: Models trained by trial and reward learned to try an approach, notice it failing, and switch to another.

source.title: Learning to reason with LLMs

toolcalling.intro: A model that can reason can also decide when to ask a specialist for help.

nodes.name: ReAct
nodes.gist: A language model could alternate between reasoning and acting: call a tool, read what came back, and carry on.

source.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

nodes.name: Toolformer
nodes.gist: A model taught itself when to call a calculator or a search engine, and how to use the answer.

source.title: Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools

nodes.name: Function calling
nodes.gist: Developers could describe tools to a model, which would then ask for one to be called and read the result.

source.title: Function calling and other API updates

nodes.name: Model Context Protocol
nodes.gist: An open standard let developers connect tools and data to AI models through one protocol, not a custom connector for each.

source.title: Introducing the Model Context Protocol

uncertainty.intro: Machines have since learned to say how sure they are, and to be tested on whether they are right.

nodes.name: Bayesian networks
nodes.gist: Probability became the standard way for a machine to say how sure it is, and to update that as evidence arrives.

source.title: Probabilistic Reasoning in Intelligent Systems

nodes.name: Monte Carlo dropout
nodes.gist: A neural network could ask the same question many times with parts switched off, and read its uncertainty from how much the answers differed.

source.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation

nodes.name: Calibration
nodes.gist: Modern networks turned out to be overconfident, and a simple fix made “ninety percent sure” mean right nine times in ten.

source.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks

nodes.name: Semantic entropy
nodes.gist: A method for language models: sample several answers, group them by meaning, and read strong disagreement as a sign the answer may be invented.

source.title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy

explaining.intro: Explaining a machine’s answer became a field of research in its own right.

nodes.name: LIME
nodes.gist: A method could explain any single prediction by fitting a simple, readable model around it.

source.title: “Why Should I Trust You?”: Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier

nodes.name: SHAP
nodes.gist: One framework gave every input an importance value for each answer, unifying six earlier methods so explanations could be compared.

source.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions

nodes.name: Scratchpads
nodes.gist: Models that wrote out their intermediate steps got long calculations right far more often.

source.title: Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models

nodes.name: Mechanistic interpretability
nodes.gist: Researchers found millions of human-readable features inside a large language model, and showed that adjusting them changed what it said.

source.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet

ingestion.intro: Knowledge moved from being typed in to being learned from web-scale repositories of text. Literally the sum of human knowledge.

nodes.name: Common Crawl
nodes.gist: An open archive of the public web, crawled from 2008 and still growing, so collecting text became a download, not a project.

source.title: Common Crawl

nodes.name: The Transformer
nodes.gist: A design that could learn from huge amounts of text in parallel, so more text meant more computers, not more people.

source.title: Attention Is All You Need

nodes.name: Pretraining
nodes.gist: A model could first learn from raw text with no labels, then be adapted to many tasks.

source.title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training

nodes.name: Scaling laws
nodes.gist: Results improved smoothly and predictably as models, text and computing power grew.

source.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
